lessons.title: Understanding Soil Texture and Structure
lessons.body: Soil texture is the mix of sand, silt, and clay particles. Sand feels gritty, silt feels like flour, and clay feels sticky when wet. To test your soil, put a handful in a jar with water, shake it, and let it settle. Sand sinks first, then silt, then clay. After 24 hours, you can measure the layers. A loam soilâabout 40% sand, 40% silt, and 20% clayâis best for most crops because it holds water and drains well. In many parts of Africa, soils are sandy (like in the Sahel) or clayey (like in parts of the Congo Basin). Sandy soils drain fast but need frequent watering. Clay soils hold water but can become waterlogged. Structure is how soil particles stick together into crumbs. Good structure means roots can grow and water moves easily. You can improve structure by adding compost or manure. For example, add 2-3 handfuls of well-rotted manure per square meter before planting. Avoid tilling wet soil because it destroys structure. A simple test: dig a small hole, fill it with water, and see how fast it drains. If it drains in less than 30 minutes, your soil is too sandy; if it takes more than 2 hours, it's too clayey. Knowing your soil helps you choose irrigation methods. Sandy soils need drip irrigation or frequent small waterings. Clay soils can use furrow irrigation but avoid overwatering. In Africa, many smallholders have sandy soils, so adding organic matter is key. Mulching with crop residues also protects structure and reduces evaporation.

lessons.title: Soil Moisture Basics: Field Capacity and Wilting Point
lessons.body: Field capacity is the amount of water soil holds after excess water has drained away. Think of a sponge after you squeeze itâit's still wet but not dripping. Wilting point is when soil is so dry that plants can no longer pull water from it and they wilt permanently. The difference between field capacity and wilting point is called available water capacity (AWC). For sandy soil, AWC is about 5-10% by volume; for loam, 15-20%; for clay, 18-25%. To check your soil moisture, squeeze a handful. If it forms a ball and leaves a wet outline on your hand, it's near field capacity. If it crumbles and won't hold together, it's near wilting point. You can also use a simple tensiometer, a tool that measures how tightly water is held. In Africa, you can make a DIY tensiometer with a ceramic cup, a tube, and a vacuum gauge, but buying one for $20-$50 is easier. For smallholders, a cheaper method is to use a soil auger or a spade to dig 15 cm deep and feel the soil. Irrigate when soil at root depth feels dry but before plants wilt. For most crops, irrigate when 50% of available water is used. For example, if your loam soil holds 20% AWC, irrigate when it drops to 10%. This avoids stressing plants and saves water. In sandy soils, check moisture every 2-3 days; in clay, every 5-7 days. Overwatering wastes water and leaches nutrients. Underwatering reduces yields. A simple rule: if you can't squeeze a ball, it's time to water.

lessons.title: Determining Infiltration Rates
lessons.body: Infiltration is how fast water enters the soil. If water runs off instead of soaking in, you're wasting water and causing erosion. To test infiltration, use a tin can with both ends removed. Push it 5 cm into the soil, pour in 2.5 cm of water, and time how long it takes to disappear. Do this three times. The rate is the depth divided by time. For example, if 2.5 cm soaks in in 10 minutes, that's 0.25 cm per minute. Sandy soils infiltrate at 2.5 cm/hour or more; loams at 1-2 cm/hour; clays at less than 0.5 cm/hour. If your rate is very low, you may need to improve soil structure with compost or use drip irrigation. High infiltration (sandy) means you need to water more often but in smaller amounts. In Africa, many soils are crusted or compacted from overgrazing or plowing. To improve infiltration, add organic matter, avoid tilling wet soil, and plant cover crops like cowpeas or lablab. You can also make small basins around plants to hold water. For furrow irrigation, the furrow length and slope affect infiltration. A slope of 0.5-2% is ideal; steeper slopes cause runoff. If infiltration is too fast, you can add clay or compost. If too slow, add sand or gypsum. A simple infiltration test helps you decide how long to run your irrigation. For example, if your soil takes in 1 cm/hour and you need to apply 3 cm of water, you must run your sprinkler for 3 hours. Without this test, you might overwater or underwater. Always test before planting and after heavy rains.

lessons.title: Crop Water Requirements and Evapotranspiration
lessons.body: Crop water requirement is the amount of water a crop needs from planting to harvest. It depends on the crop, climate, and growth stage. Evapotranspiration (ET) is water lost from soil evaporation and plant transpiration. In hot, dry areas, ET can be 5-8 mm per day; in humid areas, 2-4 mm per day. To estimate ET, use a simple pan evaporimeter: a shallow pan filled with water. Measure how much water evaporates in 24 hours. Multiply by a crop factor (0.6-1.2 depending on crop and stage) to get crop water use. For example, if pan evaporation is 6 mm and your maize is at tasseling (factor 1.1), crop water use is 6.6 mm. That means you need to apply 6.6 liters per square meter per day. For a 10 m x 10 m plot, that's 660 liters daily. In Africa, many smallholders grow maize, sorghum, millet, cowpea, and vegetables. Maize needs 500-800 mm total; sorghum 400-600 mm; cowpea 300-500 mm. Critical periods: maize needs most water at tasseling and silking; sorghum at booting and flowering; vegetables throughout. You can reduce ET by mulching, which cuts evaporation by 30-50%. Also, water early morning or evening to reduce evaporation. Drip irrigation saves water by applying it directly to roots. If you don't have a pan, use a simple rule: if the top 5 cm of soil is dry, irrigate. But for better accuracy, keep a daily record of rainfall and irrigation. A rain gauge costs $5-$10. Knowing crop water needs helps you avoid over- or under-irrigation, which can reduce yields by 20-50%.

lessons.title: Identifying Critical Irrigation Periods for Common Crops
lessons.body: Critical irrigation periods are when water shortage causes the biggest yield loss. For maize, the most critical stage is tasseling and silking (about 60-70 days after planting). Water stress then can cut yields by 50%. Next is grain filling. For sorghum, critical periods are booting (when the head emerges) and flowering. For millet, it's flowering and grain filling. For cowpea, it's flowering and pod filling. For tomatoes, it's flowering and fruit set; for onions, it's bulb formation. In Africa, many smallholders grow these crops. To manage critical periods, plan your irrigation schedule. For example, if you grow maize in a dry area, ensure you have enough water during tasseling. If water is scarce, prioritize that stage. You can use a simple calendar: mark planting date, then count days to critical stages. For maize, tasseling at 60 days, silking at 65 days. For sorghum, booting at 50 days, flowering at 60 days. For cowpea, flowering at 40 days, pod fill at 55 days. During these periods, check soil moisture daily. If the top 10 cm is dry, irrigate. Apply enough water to wet the root zone (about 30 cm deep). For sandy soil, water every 2-3 days; for clay, every 5-7 days. Avoid waterlogging, which can also reduce yields. In many parts of Africa, rainfall is erratic, so supplemental irrigation is key. Even small amounts (10-20 mm) at critical stages can make a big difference. For example, a 10 mm irrigation at maize tasseling can increase yields by 20%. Use mulch to conserve moisture. If you have a drip system, run it daily during critical periods. Keep records to learn your crop's needs.

lessons.title: Simple Tools for Soil Moisture Monitoring
lessons.body: You don't need expensive equipment to monitor soil moisture. The cheapest tool is your hand. Dig 15 cm deep with a spade, take a handful of soil, and squeeze. If it forms a ball and leaves a wet outline, it's at field capacity. If it forms a ball but no outline, it's slightly dry. If it crumbles, it's near wilting point. Do this every 2-3 days. A second tool is a soil auger or a metal pipe to take samples at different depths. A third tool is a tensiometer, which measures soil water tension. You can buy one for $20-$50 or make a simple one with a ceramic cup, a tube, and a vacuum gauge. Place it at root depth (15-30 cm). Readings: 0-10 centibars (wet), 10-30 (moist), 30-60 (dry, irrigate), above 60 (too dry). A fourth tool is a gypsum block, which works like a tensiometer but is cheaper. A fifth tool is a simple moisture meter that you push into the soil; these cost $10-$20 but can be inaccurate. For smallholders, the hand feel method plus a rain gauge is enough. A rain gauge costs $5-$10 and helps you track rainfall. You can also use a calendar to record irrigation and rainfall. In Africa, many farmers use a stick or a machete to check moisture. Push a clean metal rod into the soil; if it goes in easily, soil is moist; if hard, dry. Another method: use a bottle with a cloth wick buried in the soil; check if the cloth is wet. Combine methods for accuracy. Always check before and after irrigation. Keep a notebook. This helps you learn your soil and crops. Over time, you'll know exactly when to irrigate without tools.

quiz.q: What is the best soil texture for most crops?
quiz.explanation: Loam holds water and drains well, making it ideal for most crops.

quiz.q: How can you test soil texture at home?
quiz.explanation: The jar test separates sand, silt, and clay layers.

quiz.q: What does field capacity mean?
options: B) Soil holds all water it can after drainage
D) Soil has no available water
quiz.explanation: Field capacity is the water remaining after excess drains.

quiz.q: What is the wilting point?
options: B) When soil is at field capacity
quiz.explanation: At wilting point, plants cannot extract water and wilt permanently.

quiz.q: Which soil has the highest available water capacity?
quiz.explanation: Clay holds more water than sand or loam, but not all is available.

quiz.q: How often should you check soil moisture in sandy soil?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils drain quickly, so check more frequently.

quiz.q: What is infiltration?
quiz.explanation: Infiltration is the process of water entering the soil surface.

quiz.q: Which soil has the fastest infiltration rate?
quiz.explanation: Sand has large pores, so water enters quickly.

quiz.q: How can you improve infiltration in compacted soil?
quiz.explanation: Compost improves soil structure and pore space.

quiz.q: What is evapotranspiration?
options: A) Water lost from soil and plants
quiz.explanation: Evapotranspiration combines evaporation and plant transpiration.

quiz.q: How can you estimate crop water use?
quiz.explanation: Pan evaporation multiplied by crop factor estimates water use.

quiz.q: What is the critical irrigation period for maize?
quiz.explanation: Water stress at tasseling and silking causes major yield loss.

quiz.q: Which crop needs the most total water?
quiz.explanation: Maize typically needs 500-800 mm, more than others listed.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for soil moisture monitoring?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing soil in your hand gives a quick moisture estimate.

quiz.q: What does a tensiometer measure?
quiz.explanation: Tensiometers measure how tightly water is held in soil.

quiz.q: At what tensiometer reading should you irrigate?
quiz.explanation: 30-60 centibars indicates dry soil; irrigate before it gets drier.

quiz.q: What is the best time to irrigate to reduce evaporation?
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce water loss to evaporation.

quiz.q: What is a cheap rain gauge?
quiz.explanation: A simple tin can collect and measure rainfall depth.

quiz.q: How does mulching help with soil moisture?
quiz.explanation: Mulch covers soil and reduces water loss to evaporation.

quiz.q: What is the critical period for cowpea?
quiz.explanation: Water stress at flowering and pod fill reduces yield most.

quiz.q: How deep should you check soil moisture for most crops?
quiz.explanation: Most roots are in top 15-30 cm, so check there.

quiz.q: What is a gypsum block used for?
quiz.explanation: Gypsum blocks measure soil water tension like tensiometers.

quiz.q: What is the available water capacity of sandy soil?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils hold little available water, about 5-10% by volume.

quiz.q: What is the first step in determining infiltration rate?
options: A) Push a tin can into soil
quiz.explanation: A tin can with both ends removed is used to contain water.

quiz.q: How can you improve soil structure?
quiz.explanation: Compost adds organic matter that binds soil particles.

quiz.q: What is the crop factor for maize at tasseling?
quiz.explanation: Maize at tasseling has a high crop factor around 1.1.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to check if soil is at field capacity?
quiz.explanation: If soil forms a ball and leaves a wet outline, it's near field capacity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a critical period for sorghum?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum is most sensitive to water stress at booting and flowering.

quiz.q: What is the best way to avoid overwatering?
options: A) Check soil moisture before irrigating
quiz.explanation: Checking soil moisture prevents applying unnecessary water.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure rainfall?
quiz.explanation: A rain gauge measures the depth of rainfall.
